title: Hiccups After Drinking: Why Alcohol Causes Them and How to Stop
excerpt: Why do you get hiccups when you drink? How alcohol, fizzy drinks, and reflux trigger the hiccup reflex, the tricks that stop drunk hiccups, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why does alcohol give you hiccups? How drinking triggers the hiccup reflex, simple ways to stop drunk hiccups, how to prevent them, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why does alcohol give you hiccups
content:
**The quick answer:** hiccups after drinking are a reflex, and alcohol pokes at that reflex from several directions at once. It irritates your esophagus and stomach, it loosens the valve that keeps stomach acid down, and it dulls the part of your brain that normally keeps reflexes in check. Add the gas from beer, champagne, or soda mixers and the air you swallow when you drink fast, and your stomach stretches up against the muscle and nerves that control breathing. That is usually all it is. Drunk hiccups are almost always harmless and stop within minutes.

**What helps most:** pause the drinking, switch to plain water, and try one of the simple tricks below (holding your breath, slowly sipping cold water, a spoonful of sugar). To prevent them, drink more slowly, eat first, and go easy on fizzy drinks.

> **When to see a doctor.** Hiccups are rarely a medical problem on their own, but **see a doctor if** your hiccups last longer than 48 hours, keep coming back for days, stop you from eating, drinking, or sleeping, or come with heartburn that won't settle, trouble swallowing, or weight loss you can't explain. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** hiccups come with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, severe belly pain, sudden weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking. **If someone who has been drinking is hiccuping and vomiting while confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake,** treat it as possible alcohol poisoning: turn them on their side, stay with them, and call 911. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What a Hiccup Actually Is

A hiccup is two things happening at almost the same moment. First, your **diaphragm**, the dome-shaped muscle under your lungs that you breathe with, suddenly contracts, so you pull in a quick gulp of air. Then, a split second later, the **glottis** (the opening between your vocal cords) snaps shut. Air slams against the closed opening, and that's the "hic" sound.

This is controlled by a reflex loop, a bit like the knee-jerk you get when a doctor taps below your kneecap. The loop has three parts:

1. **Sensors.** Nerves in your throat, esophagus, stomach, and chest pick up irritation, stretching, temperature changes, or acid. The main ones are branches of the **vagus nerve**, a long nerve that runs from your brainstem down to your gut, and the **phrenic nerve**, which controls the diaphragm.
2. **A control center.** A hiccup center in the brainstem receives those signals and decides whether to fire.
3. **The output.** Signals go back down the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm, and to the muscles that close the glottis.

Anything that irritates the sensors, or that weakens the brain's usual dampening of the reflex, makes hiccups more likely. Alcohol happens to do both.

## Why Alcohol Gives You Hiccups

There isn't one single cause. Doctors usually describe several overlapping triggers, and on a typical night out you might be hitting all of them.

### 1. Gas and swallowed air stretch your stomach

This is the most common and best-understood trigger. When your stomach gets suddenly stretched, it pushes up against the diaphragm and sets off the vagus nerve. That is why big meals and fizzy drinks are classic hiccup triggers even without alcohol.

Drinking adds to the stretch in a few ways:

- **Carbonation.** Beer, champagne, prosecco, hard seltzer, and anything mixed with soda, tonic, or ginger beer releases carbon dioxide gas in your stomach.
- **Swallowed air.** Chugging, drinking through a straw, talking a lot while you drink, and shotgunning a can all send extra air down with the liquid.
- **Volume.** Beer in particular means a lot of liquid in a short time.

### 2. Alcohol irritates the esophagus and stomach

Strong alcohol is an irritant. A neat shot of spirits can feel hot on the way down for a reason: it irritates the lining of your throat and esophagus, and the nerve endings there are part of the hiccup reflex. That's why some people hiccup right after a shot, especially a very cold one. The sudden temperature change is itself a known trigger, which is also why gulping an icy drink can set them off.

### 3. Acid reflux

Alcohol relaxes the **lower esophageal sphincter**, the ring of muscle that acts as a one-way valve at the top of your stomach. When it loosens, stomach acid can splash up into the esophagus. That acid irritates the same nerve endings, and reflux is one of the most common causes of hiccups that keep coming back. Alcohol also tends to increase stomach acid, and late-night food plus lying down soon after drinking makes reflux more likely. If you notice a burning feeling in your chest along with the hiccups, reflux is a likely part of the picture. Our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers that side in detail.

### 4. Alcohol loosens the brain's brakes on the reflex

Your brain doesn't only trigger reflexes. It also holds many of them back. Alcohol is a depressant that dampens the higher parts of the brain that normally keep some reflexes in check. One common explanation for why people hiccup more as they get drunker is that this braking gets weaker, so the hiccup center fires more easily in response to triggers it would usually ignore. This part is more of a reasonable theory than a fully proven mechanism, but it fits with how often hiccups show up as people get more intoxicated.

### 5. Eating and drinking fast, and the excitement of a night out

Big, fast meals, spicy food, laughing hard, and excitement or nervousness are all listed among the everyday hiccup triggers. Bar food, late-night pizza, hot wings, and a loud, lively evening stack the odds further.

## Which Drinks Cause the Most Hiccups?

No study ranks drinks by how many hiccups they cause, so take this as a practical guide based on the triggers above rather than a measured league table.

| Drink | Why it can trigger hiccups | Lower-hiccup swap |
|---|---|---|
| Beer and cider | Carbonation plus a large volume of liquid | Sip slowly, pour into a glass to release some fizz |
| Champagne, prosecco, sparkling wine | Lots of fine bubbles, often drunk quickly at celebrations | Small pours, still wine instead |
| Hard seltzer and spiked sparkling water | Carbonation, easy to drink fast | Still water between cans |
| Spirits with soda, tonic, or ginger beer | Carbonated mixer plus irritating alcohol | Mix with still juice or water instead |
| Straight shots | Strong alcohol and often ice-cold, hitting the esophagus all at once | Sip spirits slowly instead of shooting them |
| Frozen or very cold drinks | Sudden cold on the esophagus | Let it warm slightly, drink slowly |
| Anything through a straw or chugged | Extra swallowed air | Drink from the glass, at a slower pace |

If you notice a clear pattern, such as hiccups after every beer but never after wine, the fix is usually as simple as changing what you drink or how fast you drink it.

## How to Stop Hiccups After Drinking

Most hiccup cures work, if they work at all, by doing one of two things: raising carbon dioxide in your blood a little (which seems to calm the diaphragm), or giving the vagus nerve a different, stronger signal to deal with so the reflex loop resets. Honest caveat: there is very little solid research on home hiccup remedies. Most of what we know comes from experience and small reports, not controlled trials. The good news is that the common tricks are harmless for most people, so it's reasonable to try a couple.

### Step one: stop drinking for a bit

The simplest move is the one people skip. Put the drink down for 15 to 20 minutes. If you keep adding fizzy or strong alcohol, you're feeding the trigger while trying to fix it. Switch to plain still water, sipped rather than gulped.

### Breathing tricks

- **Hold your breath.** Take a normal breath in and hold it for about 10 to 20 seconds, then breathe out slowly. Repeat a few times if needed. Don't strain or hold until you feel faint, especially if you've been drinking.
- **Breathe in and hold, then breathe in a little more.** Take a deep breath, hold for about 10 seconds, then sip in a bit more air without breathing out, hold again, and repeat once more. Many people find this works better than a single hold.
- **Slow, steady breathing.** Breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six or eight for a minute or two. This is gentle and safe even if you're tipsy.
- **Breathing into a paper bag.** This raises carbon dioxide slightly. Only use a paper bag (never plastic), only for a short time, and skip it if you have heart or lung problems or feel dizzy. It isn't a good choice for someone who's very drunk.

### Swallowing tricks

These give the throat and vagus nerve a new job, which can interrupt the reflex.

- **Sip cold water slowly and steadily**, taking several small swallows in a row without stopping for breath.
- **Drink from the far side of a glass** by leaning forward. It forces slow, careful swallowing. Do this sitting down, not after several drinks while standing.
- **Swallow a teaspoon of granulated sugar** dry. The gritty texture stimulates the back of the throat. It's one of the oldest home remedies, and it's harmless for most people.
- **Bite into a lemon wedge or take a tiny sip of vinegar.** The sharp taste is another strong signal to the throat. Rinse your mouth with water afterwards to protect your teeth, and skip vinegar if you already have heartburn.
- **Gargle with cold water** for 20 to 30 seconds.

A straw-shaped device designed to make you suck hard against resistance while swallowing (sold as HiccAway) was studied in a 2021 survey-based report in *JAMA Network Open*. Users reported good results, but the study had no comparison group and relied on self-reports, so it's encouraging rather than conclusive. A regular glass of water, sipped steadily, uses much the same idea.

### Body position tricks

- **Pull your knees to your chest** while sitting, and lean forward for about two minutes. This gently compresses the chest and diaphragm.
- **Lean forward** to put light pressure on your diaphragm.
- **Press gently just below your breastbone** while you breathe out slowly.

### What not to do

- **Don't try to scare someone who's drunk.** It rarely works, and a startled, unsteady person can fall.
- **Don't do "upside-down" water drinking** if you've been drinking. It's a choking and falling risk.
- **Don't keep drinking fizzy drinks or shots** to "push through" them.
- **Don't take sedating sleep or allergy medicine** to sleep off hiccups after drinking. Alcohol is already a sedative, and the combination can make you far more drowsy than you expect.

## Hiccups and Heavy Drinking: When It's More Than Just Hiccups

For most social drinkers, hiccups are a mild nuisance. But there are a few situations where they deserve more attention.

### Hiccups plus vomiting in someone very drunk

Hiccups, retching, and vomiting often travel together after heavy drinking, because the same overfull, irritated stomach drives all three. The real danger isn't the hiccup. It's that someone who is barely conscious can vomit and inhale it.

If you're looking after someone in that state:

- **Keep them sitting up or lying on their side**, never flat on their back.
- **Don't give them anything to eat or drink** if they're very drowsy or struggling to stay awake.
- **Stay with them.**
- **Call 911** if they can't be woken, are confused, have slow or irregular breathing, have pale or bluish skin, feel very cold, or are vomiting while not fully awake. Don't wait for every sign to appear. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) lays them out plainly.

### Hiccups that last for days

Doctors sort hiccups by how long they last. A normal bout lasts minutes to a few hours. Hiccups that go on for more than **48 hours** are called **persistent**, and those lasting more than a month are called **intractable**. Long-lasting hiccups are uncommon, but when they happen they're worth checking out, because they can be linked to things like reflux disease, stomach or esophagus problems, nerve irritation, certain medicines, kidney problems, or, rarely, conditions affecting the brain, chest, or heart.

Heavy, regular alcohol use is one of the recognized contributors to persistent hiccups, largely through reflux and stomach irritation. If you're getting hiccups that drag on for days after drinking, it's a good reason to see a doctor, partly to look for reflux or stomach irritation that may need treatment, and partly to rule out other causes. For stubborn cases, doctors have prescription options. Chlorpromazine is the medicine most often cited as FDA-approved for hiccups, and doctors also use others, such as baclofen or gabapentin, off-label. These are for a doctor to decide, not for self-treatment.

### Hiccups with chest pain or trouble breathing

In rare cases, hiccups can show up alongside a heart or lung problem. If your hiccups come with chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, shortness of breath, sweating, or feeling faint, treat it as an emergency and call 911. Don't assume it's just the drinks.

## Hiccups the Morning After

Some people notice hiccups the next day rather than at the bar. A few things can explain that:

- **Lingering reflux.** Alcohol can keep the stomach valve relaxed and the stomach lining irritated for hours. Lying down after a late night of drinking and eating makes reflux worse, and reflux is a known hiccup trigger.
- **An irritated, sensitive stomach.** Many hangovers involve an upset stomach, and the same nerve pathways are involved. If you're also dealing with cramps or an ache, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) can help you work out what's going on.
- **What you reach for.** Coffee on an empty stomach, fizzy electrolyte drinks, or a greasy breakfast eaten fast can all set them off again.

What tends to help the morning after:

- Eat something small and bland, like toast, crackers, a banana, or oatmeal.
- Sip still water or an electrolyte drink slowly rather than gulping.
- Hold off on coffee until you've eaten, and skip carbonated drinks for a few hours.
- Stay upright for a while after eating.
- If heartburn is part of it, an over-the-counter antacid used as the label directs is reasonable for most healthy adults. Check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

If hiccups keep returning for more than two days, see a doctor.

## Why Do Some People Hiccup After Just One Drink?

If one beer reliably gives you hiccups, it usually comes down to the drink and the way you drink it rather than how much alcohol you've had. Common reasons:

- **You're sensitive to carbonation.** Some people's stomachs react strongly to a little gas.
- **You drink the first one fast.** The first drink is often the thirstiest one.
- **You're drinking on an empty stomach.** Alcohol hits an empty stomach harder and irritates it more. Our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why eating first changes how your body handles the night.
- **You already have reflux.** If you get heartburn easily, even a small amount of alcohol can be enough to set off acid and hiccups.
- **The temperature shock.** A very cold first sip on a hot day is a trigger in its own right.

Getting hiccups after one drink is not, by itself, a sign of alcohol intolerance or a medical problem. If it comes with flushing, a stuffy nose, hives, or feeling unwell quickly, that's a different pattern worth reading about, and worth mentioning to a doctor.

## How to Prevent Hiccups When You Drink

Prevention is mostly about removing the triggers before they stack up:

1. **Eat before you drink.** A meal slows how quickly alcohol reaches the stomach lining and bloodstream, and you're less likely to chug on an empty stomach.
2. **Slow down.** Aim for sipping rather than gulping. A glass of water between drinks helps naturally.
3. **Cut the fizz.** If you hiccup with beer or bubbly, try still wine, spirits with still mixers, or a lower-fizz option. Letting a beer sit in a glass for a minute releases some gas.
4. **Skip the straw and the shotgun.** Both add swallowed air.
5. **Watch the temperature.** Very icy drinks and frozen cocktails are worth sipping slowly.
6. **Go easy on spicy food** if spicy wings or hot sauce tend to set you off.
7. **Don't lie down right after drinking and eating.** Stay upright for a while to keep acid where it belongs.
8. **Drink less overall.** Fewer drinks mean less stomach irritation, less reflux, and less loosening of the brain's reflex brakes. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing and other habits that help the whole night, not just the hiccups.

## A Note on Hangover Supplements

You might wonder whether anything you take before or during a night out can stop the hiccups. There is no good evidence that any supplement prevents or treats alcohol-related hiccups, including DHM. The steps that actually help are the ones above: eat, slow down, and drink less fizz.

Where DHM (dihydromyricetin) comes in is the broader hangover picture. It's a plant compound studied for its possible effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and it doesn't replace drinking less. If you'd like to try it for the next-day side of a night out, two common picks are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Hiccups after drinking are a reflex triggered by a stretched, irritated stomach, acid reflux, cold or strong drinks, and alcohol's dampening effect on the brain's reflex control.
- Carbonated drinks, drinking fast, straws, and an empty stomach make them more likely.
- To stop them, pause the drinking, sip water, and try a simple breathing or swallowing trick. None works every time, but they're harmless.
- To prevent them, eat first, slow down, and cut back on fizz.
- See a doctor if hiccups last more than 48 hours or come with heartburn that won't settle or trouble swallowing. Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting blood, or a very drunk person who is vomiting and hard to wake.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get hiccups when I drink alcohol?**

Hiccups are a reflex spasm of the diaphragm, and drinking sets off that reflex in several ways at once. Alcohol irritates the esophagus and stomach, relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach so acid can creep up, and lowers the brain's normal braking of reflexes. Carbonated drinks and drinking quickly also stretch the stomach with gas and swallowed air, which presses on the diaphragm and the nerves that control it.

**How do you stop drunk hiccups fast?**

Stop drinking for a while, then try a simple trick that interrupts the reflex: hold your breath for 10 to 20 seconds, slowly sip a glass of cold water without stopping, swallow a teaspoon of sugar, or sit and pull your knees to your chest. There is no good evidence that any single trick works for everyone, but they are harmless and often work. If the person is very drunk, keep them sitting up and don't give them anything to swallow if they are drowsy or vomiting.

**Are hiccups a sign you are too drunk?**

Not on their own. Many people hiccup after one beer or one fizzy cocktail. But hiccups that start as you drink more, especially along with slurred speech, stumbling, or nausea, are a reasonable cue to stop drinking and switch to water. Hiccups plus vomiting, confusion, or being hard to wake are signs of possible alcohol poisoning, and you should call 911.

**Why do some drinks give me hiccups more than others?**

Carbonation is the most common culprit. Beer, champagne, hard seltzer, and cocktails made with soda or tonic fill the stomach with gas, and a stretched stomach is a classic hiccup trigger. Very strong or very cold shots can also irritate the esophagus on the way down, and drinking through a straw or chugging adds swallowed air.

**How long do alcohol hiccups usually last?**

Usually a few minutes, sometimes up to an hour or so. Hiccups that keep coming back for more than 48 hours are called persistent hiccups and are worth a doctor's visit, whether or not alcohol seems to be the trigger.

**Can hiccups the next day be part of a hangover?**

They can. Alcohol can leave the stomach lining irritated and make acid reflux worse into the next morning, and reflux is a known hiccup trigger. Eating something bland, sipping water slowly, and avoiding more fizzy drinks or coffee on an empty stomach usually helps. If they last more than two days, see a doctor.

**Can drunk hiccups be dangerous?**

The hiccups themselves are almost always harmless. The danger comes from what can happen alongside them when someone is very drunk: hiccups and retching can lead to vomiting, and a person who is barely conscious can choke. Never leave a very drunk person lying on their back. Put them on their side, stay with them, and call 911 if they are hard to wake or breathing slowly or irregularly.

**Does DHM stop hiccups?**

There is no good evidence that DHM has any effect on hiccups. DHM is studied for how it may affect alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. For hiccups, the most reliable steps are drinking more slowly, cutting back on carbonated drinks, and eating before you drink.
